Legal Classification of Reimbursements for Property Improvements In the context of an inheritance division, a co-heir requested compensation for improvements made to a common property. The legal issue concerns whether such a claim falls under Art. 1150 c.c. (indemnity for value increase) or general mandate rules. The interpretative challenge lies in the nature of the co-heir's possession. The Court applied the principle that a co-heir is not a third-party possessor but acts as a "negotiorum gestor" (manager of others' affairs). Consequently, they are entitled only to the reimbursement of actual expenses for materials and labor, excluding monetary revaluation, as the obligation is classified as a "debt of currency" (debito di valuta) rather than a "debt of value".
Evidentiary Standards for Inheritance Reimbursement Claims The plaintiff sought reimbursement for works valued at €45,000, presenting various receipts and invoices. The legal problem involves the burden of proof regarding the certainty and relevance of expenses. The interpretative difficulty arises when documentation is generic or contradictory. The Court ruled that reimbursement requires strict and specific evidence. In this case, the claim was rejected because invoices were addressed to a different street number than the inherited property, and many receipts were illegible or lacked descriptions of the materials purchased, making it impossible to link the costs to the specific estate asset.
